entries.17ad1282df3851f190c05836cf6cf76e32e8693b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6804"/><div sID="gen10439" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6804"/>28-31. In confidence that God's blessing would come on him, and confusion and shame on his enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.13">Psa 73:13</reference>), he ceases to regard their curses, and anticipates a season of joyful and public thanksgiving; for God is near to protect (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.8">Psa 16:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.6">34:6</reference>) the poor from all unrighteous judges who may condemn him. <chapter eID="Ps.109"/>

entries.598e77cdba99889e907ebd46ae13c8cdae819f4a: <div eID="gen22312" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22313" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22314" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22314" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22313" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22315" type="x-p"/> The psalmist speaks against his inveterate enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.109.1-Psa.109.5">Psa 109:1-5</reference>. He prays against them, and denounces God's judgments, <reference osisRef="Psa.109.6-Psa.109.15">Psa 109:6-15</reference>. The reason on which this is grounded, <reference osisRef="Psa.109.16-Psa.109.20">Psa 109:16-20</reference>. He prays for his own safety and salvation, using many arguments to induce God to have mercy upon him, <reference osisRef="Psa.109.21-Psa.109.31">Psa 109:21-31</reference>. <div eID="gen22315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22316" type="x-p"/> The title of this Psalm, To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David, has already often occurred, and on it the Versions offer nothing new. The Syriac says it is "a Psalm of David, when the people, without his knowledge, made Absalom king; on which account he was slain: but to us (Christians) he details the passion of Christ." That it contains a prophecy against Judas and the enemies of our Lord, is evident from <reference osisRef="Act.1.20">Act 1:20</reference>. Probably, in its primary meaning, (for such a meaning it certainly has), it may refer to Ahithophel. The execrations in it should be rendered in the future tense, as they are mere prophetic denunciations of God's displeasure against sinners. Taken in this light, it cannot be a stumbling-block to any person. God has a right to denounce those judgments which he will inflict on the workers of iniquity. But perhaps the whole may be the execrations of David's enemies against himself. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.109.20">Psa 109:20</reference> (note). Ahithophel, who gave evil counsel against David, and being frustrated hanged himself, was no mean prototype of Judas the traitor; it was probably on this account that St. Peter, <reference osisRef="Act.1.20">Act 1:20</reference>, applied it to the case of Judas, as a prophetic declaration concerning him, or at least a subject that might be accommodated to his case. <div eID="gen22316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22317" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22318" type="x-p"/> Hold not thy peace - Be not silent; arise and defend my cause.
entries.fc655fb1774c8fa0ff616807f86044933da3763d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22319" type="x-p"/> The mouth of the wicked and - the deceitful are opened against me - Many persons are continually uttering calumnies against me. Thou knowest my heart and its innocence; vindicate my uprightness against these calumniators.
entries.59562b72d1b1d199d3134bfb7e607e5c160ae793: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen22319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22320" type="x-p"/> For my love they are my adversaries - In their behalf I have performed many acts of kindness, and they are my adversaries notwithstanding; this shows principles the most vicious, and hearts the most corrupt. Many of the fathers and commentators have understood the principal part of the things spoken here as referring to our Lord, and the treatment he received from the Jews; and whatever the original intention was, they may safely be applied to this case, as the <reference osisRef="Psa.109.2">Psa 109:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.109.3">Psa 109:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.109.4">Psa 109:4</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.109.5">Psa 109:5</reference> are as highly illustrative of the conduct of the Jewish rulers towards our Lord as the following verses are of the conduct of Judas; but allowing these passages to be prophetic, it is the Jewish state rather than an individual, against which these awful denunciations are made, as it seems to be represented here under the person and character of an extremely hardened and wicked man; unless we consider the curses to be those of David's enemies. See the note on <reference osisRef="Psa.109.20">Psa 109:20</reference> (note). <div eID="gen22320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22321" type="x-p"/> But I give myself unto prayer - ואני תפלה vaani thephillah; "And I prayer." The Chaldee: ואנא אצלי vaana atsalley, "but I pray." This gives a good sense, which is followed by the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon. The Syriac, "I will pray for them." This, not so correctly; as dreadful imprecations, not prayers, follow. But probably the whole ought to be interpreted according to the mode laid down, <reference osisRef="Psa.109.20">Psa 109:20</reference>. The translation and paraphrase in the old Psalter are very simple: - <div eID="gen22321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22322" type="x-p"/> Trans. For that thyng that thai sulde hafe lufed me, thai bakbited me; bot I prayed. <div eID="gen22322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22323" type="x-p"/> Par - That is, that sulde haf lufed me for I was godson, and thai bakbited me sayande, in Belzebub he castes oute fendes; bot I prayed for thaim.
entries.08e9250f2de23c5a23e8fe841e1aa2979a37f4cc: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen22323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22324" type="x-p"/> Let Satan stand at his right hand - As the word שטן satan means an adversary simply, though sometimes it is used to express the evil spirit Satan, I think it best to preserve here its grammatical meaning: "Let an adversary stand at his right hand:" i.e., Let him be opposed and thwarted in all his purposes. <div eID="gen22324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22325" type="x-p"/> All the Versions have devil, or some equivocal word. The Arabic has eblees, the chief of the apostate spirits; but the name is probably corrupted from the Greek διαβολος diabolos; from which the Latin diabolus. the Italian diavolo, the Spanish diablo, the French diable, the Irish or Celtic diabal, the Dutch duivel, the German teufel, the Anglo-Saxon deofal, and the English devil, are all derived. The original, διαβολος, comes from δια βαλλειν to shoot or pierce through.
entries.f0d04157c73feb4d0355be41b5604e24ccbec897: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22326" type="x-p"/> Let him be condemned - יצא רשע yetse rasha. "Let him come out a wicked man;" that is let his wickedness be made manifest. <div eID="gen22326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22327" type="x-p"/> Let his prayer become sin - Thus paraphrased by Calmet: "Let him be accused, convicted, and condemned, and let the defense which he brings for his justification only serve to deepen his guilt, and hasten his condemnation." I once more apprise the reader, that if these are not the words of David's enemies against himself, (see on <reference osisRef="Psa.109.20">Psa 109:20</reference> (note)), they are prophetic denunciations against a rebellious and apostate person or people, hardened in crime, and refusing to return to God.
entries.be85c3f2a0e4b196ed81676445e5bebd279b2c38: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen22327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22328" type="x-p"/> Let another take his office - The original is פקדתו pekuddatho, which the margin translates charge, and which literally means superintendence, oversight, inspection from actual visitations. The translation in our common Version is too technical. His bishopric, following the Septuagint, επισκοπην, and Vulgate, episcopatum and has given cause to some light people to be witty, who have said, "The first bishop we read of was bishop Judas." But it would be easy to convict this witticism of blasphemy, as the word is used in many parts of the sacred writings, from Genesis downward, to signify offices and officers, appointed either by God immediately, or in the course of his providence, for the accomplishment of the most important purposes. It is applied to the patriarch Joseph, <reference osisRef="Gen.39.4">Gen 39:4</reference>, ויפקדהו vaiyaphkidehu, he made him bishop, alias overseer; therefore it might be as wisely said, and much more correctly, "The first bishop we read of was bishop Joseph;" and many such bishops there were of God's making long before Judas was born. After all, Judas was no traitor when he was appointed to what is called his bishopric, office, or charge in the apostolate. Such witticisms as these amount to no argument, and serve no cause that is worthy of defense. <div eID="gen22328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22329" type="x-p"/> Our common Version, however, was not the first to use the word: it stands in the Anglo-Saxon "and his episcopacy let take other." The old Psalter is nearly the same; I shall give the whole verse: Fa be made his days, and his bysshopryk another take. "For Mathai was sett in stede of Judas; and his days was fa that hynged himself."
entries.69b2ed263e1de1ef084c20cf731ea8239e2a485d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen22329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22330" type="x-p"/> Let his children be fatherless, etc. - It is said that Judas was a married man, against whom this verse, as well as the preceding is supposed to be spoken; and that it was to support them that he stole from the bag in which the property of the apostles was put, and of which he was the treasurer.
entries.55442e54c61b93b8bbeb8555286163a45d06cc18: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen22330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22331" type="x-p"/> Set his children - beg - The father having lost his office, the children must necessarily be destitute; and this is the hardest lot to which any can become subject, after having been born to the expectation of an ample fortune.
entries.a475828da2a8a8a031cc72f234e404916685e2f8: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen22331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22332" type="x-p"/> Let the strangers spoil his labor - Many of these execrations were literally fulfilled in the case of the miserable Jews, after the death of our Lord. They were not only expelled from their own country, after the destruction of Jerusalem, but they were prohibited from returning; and so taxed by the Roman government, that they were reduced to the lowest degree of poverty. Domitian expelled them from Rome; and they were obliged to take up their habitation without the gate Capena, in a wood contiguous to the city, for which they were obliged to pay a rent, and where the whole of their property was only a basket and a little hay. See Juvenal, Sat. ver. 11: - <div eID="gen22332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22333" type="x-p"/> Substitit ad veteres arcus, madidamque Capenam: <div eID="gen22333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22334" type="x-p"/> Hic ubi nocturne Numa constituebat amicae, <div eID="gen22334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22335" type="x-p"/> Nunc sacri fontis nemus, et delubra locantur <div eID="gen22335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22336" type="x-p"/> Judaes: quorum cophinus, foenumque supellex: <div eID="gen22336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22337" type="x-p"/> Omnis enim populo mercedem pendere jussa est <div eID="gen22337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22338" type="x-p"/> Arbor, et ejectis mendicat silva Camoenis. <div eID="gen22338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22339" type="x-p"/> He stopped a little at the conduit gate, <div eID="gen22339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22340" type="x-p"/> Where Numa modelled once the Roman state; <div eID="gen22340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22341" type="x-p"/> In nightly councils with his nymph retired: <div eID="gen22341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22342" type="x-p"/> Though now the sacred shades and founts are hired <div eID="gen22342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22343" type="x-p"/> By banished Jews, who their whole wealth can lay <div eID="gen22343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22344" type="x-p"/> In a small basket, on a wisp of hay. <div eID="gen22344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22345" type="x-p"/> Yet such our avarice is, that every tree <div eID="gen22345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22346" type="x-p"/> Pays for his head; nor sleep itself is free; <div eID="gen22346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22347" type="x-p"/> Nor place nor persons now are sacred held, <div eID="gen22347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22348" type="x-p"/> From their own grove the Muses are expelled. <div eID="gen22348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22349" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen22349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22350" type="x-p"/> The same poet refers again to this wretched state of the Jews, Sat. vi., ver. 541; and shows to what vile extremities they were reduced in order to get a morsel of bread: - <div eID="gen22350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22351" type="x-p"/> Cum dedit ille locum, cophino foenoque relicto, <div eID="gen22351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22352" type="x-p"/> Arcanam Judaea tremens mendicat in aurem, <div eID="gen22352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22353" type="x-p"/> Interpres legum Solymarum, et magna sacerdos <div eID="gen22353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22354" type="x-p"/> Arboris, ac summi fida internuncia coeli. <div eID="gen22354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22355" type="x-p"/> Implet et illa manum, sed parcius, aere minuto. <div eID="gen22355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22356" type="x-p"/> Qualia cunque voles Judaei somnia vendunt. <div eID="gen22356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22357" type="x-p"/> Here a Jewess is represented as coming from the wood mentioned above, to gain a few oboli by fortune-telling; and, trembling lest she should be discovered, she leaves her basket and hay, and whispers lowly in the ear of some female, from whom she hopes employment in her line. She is here called by the poet the interpretess of the laws of Solymae, or Jerusalem, and the priestess of a tree, because obliged, with the rest of her nation, to lodge in a wood; so that she and her countrymen might be said to seek their bread out of desolate places, the stranger having spoiled their labor. Perhaps the whole of the Psalm relates to their infidelities, rebellions, and the miseries inflicted on them from the crucifixion of our Lord till the present time. I should prefer this sense, if what is said on <reference osisRef="Psa.109.20">Psa 109:20</reference> be not considered a better mode of interpretation.
entries.d7d98ebff7ff088409a7685a2100eb832dccb61c: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen22357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22358" type="x-p"/> Let his posterity be cut off - It is a fact that the distinction among the Jewish tribes in entirely lost. Not a Jew in the world knows from what tribe he is sprung; and as to the royal family, it remains nowhere but in the person of Jesus the Messiah. He alone is the Lion of the tribe of Judah. Except as it exists in him, the name is blotted out.
entries.4b47cb782e9cbff10a7a9ffc0a802091388ee0d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen22358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22359" type="x-p"/> Persecuted the poor and needy man - In the case of Jesus Christ all the dictates of justice and mercy were destroyed, and they persecuted this poor man unto death. They acted from a diabolical malice. On common principles, their opposition to Christ cannot be accounted for.
entries.d84ccc6ed173c50332df9bd63454cb1bf7b63588: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen22359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22360" type="x-p"/> As he loved cursing, so let it come unto him - The Jews said, when crucifying our Lord, His blood be upon us and our children! Never was an imprecation more dreadfully fulfilled.
entries.ba109d2ba7540a486290e43d57c55519f36be586: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen22360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22361" type="x-p"/> Let it come into his bowels like water - Houbigant thinks this is an allusion to the waters of jealousy; and he is probably right, - the bitter waters that produce the curse. See <reference osisRef="Num.5.18">Num 5:18</reference>.
entries.9ea51ef6a0762249f366484347e0cdfbed7a4ddd: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen22361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22362" type="x-p"/> And for a girdle - Let the curse cleave to him throughout life: as the girdle binds all the clothes to the body, let the curse of God bind all mischiefs and maladies to his body and soul. <div eID="gen22362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22363" type="x-p"/> The Hindoos, Budhists, and others often wear a gold or silver chain about their waist. One of those chains, once the ornament of a Moudeliar in the island of Ceylon, lies now before me: it is silver, and curiously wrought.
entries.02bb62338ef816c5a8c1298a55cd98bd04f29939: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen22363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22364" type="x-p"/> Let this be the reward of mine adversaries from the Lord, and of them that speak evil apainst my soul - Following the mode of interpretation already adopted, this may mean: All these maledictions shall be fulfilled on my enemies; they shall have them for their reward. So all the opposition made by the Jews against our Lord, and the obloquies and execrations wherewith they have loaded him and his religion, have fallen upon themselves; and they are awful examples of the wrath of God abiding on them that believe not. <div eID="gen22364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22365" type="x-p"/> But is not this verse a key to all that preceded it? The original, fairly interpreted, will lead us to a somewhat different meaning: זאת פעלת שטני מאת יהוה והדברים רע על נפשי zoth peullath soteney meeth Yehovah, vehaddoberim ra al naphshi. "This is the work of my adversaries before the Lord, and of those who speak evil against my soul," or life. That is, all that is said from the sixth to the twentieth verse consists of the evil words and imprecations of my enemies against my soul, laboring to set the Lord, by imprecations, against me, that their curses may take effect. This, which is a reasonable interpretation, frees the whole Psalm from every difficulty. Surely, the curses contained in it are more like those which proceed from the mouth of the wicked, than from one inspired by tne Spirit of the living God. Taking the words in this sense, which I am persuaded is the best, and which the original will well bear and several of the Versions countenance, then our translation may stand just as it is, only let the reader remember that at the sixth verse David begins to tell how his enemies cursed Him, while he prayed for Them.
entries.a3e4fd6389e16b821dc270cb9c570e31d978ac12: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen22365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22366" type="x-p"/> But do thou for me - While they use horrible imprecations against me, and load me with their curses, act thou for me, and deliver me from their maledictions. While they curse, do thou bless. This verse is a farther proof of the correctness of the interpretation given above.
entries.16df69af86c946e06b3ac78f263e14112bdbe241: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen22366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22367" type="x-p"/> I am poor and needy - I am allicted and impoverished; and my heart is wounded - my very life is sinking through distress.
entries.97be839f936c9c1730238f4ab5c32947deb7876a: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen22367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22368" type="x-p"/> I am gone like the shadow - "I have walked like the declining shadow," - I have passed my meridian of health and life; and as the sun is going below the horizon, so am I about to go under the earth. <div eID="gen22368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22369" type="x-p"/> I am tossed up and down as the locust - When swarms of locusts take wing, and infest the countries in the east, if the wind happen to blow briskly, the swarms are agitated and driven upon each other, so as to appear to be heaved to and fro, or tossed up and down. Dr. Shaw, who has seen this, says it gives a lively idea of the comparisons of the psalmist.
entries.1286728afc3c91c348e7dec49bf2d91d7ff3d516: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen22369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22370" type="x-p"/> My knees are weak through fasting - That hunger is as soon felt in weakening the knees, as in producing an uneasy sensation in the stomach, is known by all who have ever felt it. Writers in all countries have referred to this effect of hunger. Thus Tryphioderus Il. Excid. ver 155: Τειρομενου βαρυθειεν ατερπεΐ γουνατα λιμῳ. "Their knees might fail, by hunger's force subdued; <div eID="gen22370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22371" type="x-p"/> And sink, unable to sustain their load." <div eID="gen22371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22372" type="x-p"/> Merrick. <div eID="gen22372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22373" type="x-p"/> So Plautus, Curcul, act. ii., scen. 3: - <div eID="gen22373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22374" type="x-p"/> Tenebrae oboriuntur, genua inedia succidunt. "My eyes grow dim; my knees are weak with hunger." <div eID="gen22374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22375" type="x-p"/> And Lucretius, lib. 4: ver. 950: - <div eID="gen22375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22376" type="x-p"/> Brachia, palpebraeque cadunt, poplitesque procumbunt. "The arms, the eyelids fall; the knees give way." <div eID="gen22376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22377" type="x-p"/> Both the knees and the sight are particularly affected by hunger.
entries.c0c416a94d8699655387a88b3127d88cc50c2109: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen22377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22378" type="x-p"/> When they looked upon me they soaked their heads - Thus was David treated by Shimei, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5">2Sam 16:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.6">2Sam 16:6</reference>, and our blessed Lord by the Jews, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.39">Mat 27:39</reference>.
entries.d32c1e5db742ad8f6ed0c96bfe19f6e69f06d891: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen22378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22379" type="x-p"/> That they may know that this is thy hand - Let thy help be so manifest in my behalf, that they may see it is thy hand, and that thou hast undertaken for me. Or, if the words refer to the passion of our Lord, Let them see that I suffer not on my own account; "for the transgression of my people am I smitten."
entries.ba571b2daaa4ebb68b2173c85cc502e15062dc47: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen22379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22380" type="x-p"/> Let them curse, but bless thou - See on <reference osisRef="Psa.109.20">Psa 109:20</reference> (note): Of the mode of interpretation recommended there, this verse gives additional proof.
entries.3337a6612ee4af2354d6dd3aab2f5e71d83291fa: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen22380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22381" type="x-p"/> Let them cover themselves - He here retorts their own curse, <reference osisRef="Psa.109.18">Psa 109:18</reference>.
entries.d53796c4798d7e689806ee47da2e4ae8e767086c: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen22381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22382" type="x-p"/> I will greatly praise the Lord - I have the fullest prospect of deliverance, and a plenary vindication of my innocence.
entries.80c4c10d55b9458e04b02ebde71b2e4a3464a5ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen22382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22383" type="x-p"/> He shall stand at the right hand of the poor - Even if Satan himself be the accuser, God will vindicate the innocence of his servant. Pilate and the Jews condemned our Lord to death as a malefactor; God showed his immaculate innocence by his resurrection from the dead. <div eID="gen22383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22384" type="x-p"/> The whole of this Psalm is understood by many as referring solely to Christ, the traitor Judas, and the wicked Jews. This is the view taken of it in the analysis.  <chapter eID="Ps.109"/> <div eID="gen22384" type="x-p"/>

entries.bc8d955c07717db8eb83353b2ee2904f6d8a8122: <div eID="gen10051" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Imprecation upon the Curser Who Prefers the Curse to the Blessing</title> <div sID="gen10052" type="x-p"/> The אודה, corresponding like an echo to the הודו of Ps 107, is also found here in Psa 109:30. But Psalms 109 is most closely related to Ps 69. Anger concerning the ungodly who requite love with ingratitude, who persecute innocence and desire the curse instead of the blessing, has here reached its utmost bound. The imprecations are not, however, directed against a multitude as in Ps 69, but their whole current is turned against one person. Is this Doeg the Edomite, or Cush the Benjamite? We do not know. The marks of Jeremiah’s hand, which raised a doubt about the לדוד of Ps 69, are wanting here; and if the development of the thoughts appears too diffuse and overloaded to be suited to David, and also many expressions (as the inflected מעט in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.8">Psa 109:8</reference>, the נכאה, which is explained by the Syriac, in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.16">Psa 109:16</reference>, and the half-passive חלל in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.22">Psa 109:22</reference>) look as though they belong to the later period of the language, yet we feel on the other hand the absence of any certain echoes of older models. For in the parallels <reference osisRef="Ps.109.6">Psa 109:6</reference>, cf. Zec 3:1, and <reference osisRef="Ps.109.18">Psa 109:18</reference>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.109.29">Psa 109:29</reference></hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.59.17">Isa 59:17</reference>, it is surely not the mutual relationship but the priority that is doubtful; <reference osisRef="Ps.109.22">Psa 109:22</reference>, however, in relation to <reference osisRef="Ps.55.5">Psa 55:5</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">Psa 109:4</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.55.5">Psa 55:5</reference>) is a variation such as is also allowable in one and the same poet (e.g., in the refrains). The anathemas that are here poured forth more extensively than anywhere else speak in favour of David, or at least of his situation. They are explained by the depth of David’s consciousness that he is the anointed of Jahve, and by his contemplation of himself in Christ. The persecution of David was a sin not only against David himself, but also against the Christ in him; and because Christ is in David, the outbursts of the Old Testament wrathful spirit take the prophetic form, so that this Psalm also, like Ps 22 and Ps 69, is a typically prophetic Psalm, inasmuch as the utterance of the type concerning himself is carried by the Spirit of prophecy beyond himself, and thus the ara' is raised to the προφητεία ἐν εἴδει ἀρᾶς (Chrysostom). These imprecations are not, however, appropriate in the mouth of the suffering Saviour. It is not the spirit of Zion but of Sinai which here speaks out of the mouth of David; the spirit of Elias, which, according to <reference osisRef="Luke.9.55">Luk 9:55</reference>, is not the spirit of the New Testament. This wrathful spirit is overpowered in the New Testament by the spirit of love. But these anathemas are still not on this account so many beatings of the air. There is in them a divine energy, as in the blessing and cursing of every man who is united to God, and more especially of a man whose temper of mind is such as David's. They possess the same power as the prophetical threatenings, and in this sense they are regarded in the New Testament as fulfilled in the son of perdition (Joh 17:12). To the generation of the time of Jesus they were a deterrent warning not to offend against the Holy One of God, and this <hi type="italic">Psalmus</hi> <hi type="italic">Ischarioticus</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.20">Act 1:20</reference>) will ever be such a mirror of warning to the enemies and persecutors of Christ and His Church.
entries.b8c6375026dbb16e91c54ce8769ddf63419aaf0d: <reference osisRef="Ps.109.1-Ps.109.5">Psa 109:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen10052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10053" type="x-p"/> A sign for help and complaints of ungrateful persecutors form the beginning of the Psalm. “God of my praise” is equivalent to God, who art my praise, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.14">Jer 17:14</reference>, cf. Deu 10:21. The God whom the Psalmist has hitherto had reason to praise will also now show Himself to him as worthy to be praised. Upon this faith he bases the prayer: be not silent (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.1">Psa 28:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.22">Psa 35:22</reference>)! A mouth such as belongs to the “wicked,” a mouth out of which comes “deceit,” have they opened against him; they have spoken with him a tongue (accusative, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.64.6">Psa 64:6</reference>), i.e., a language, of falsehood. דּברי of things and utterances as in Psa 35:20. It would be capricious to take the suffix of אהבתי in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">Psa 109:4</reference> as <hi type="italic">genit. object.</hi> (love which they owe me), and in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.5">Psa 109:5</reference> as <hi type="italic">genit. subject</hi>.; from <reference osisRef="Ps.38.21">Psa 38:21</reference> it may be seen that the love which he has shown to them is also meant in Psa 109:4. The assertion that he is “prayer” is intended to say that he, repudiating all revenges of himself, takes refuge in God in prayer and commits his cause into His hands. They have loaded him with evil for good, and hatred for the love he has shown to them. Twice he lays emphasis on the fact that it is love which they have requited to him with its opposite. Perfects alternate with aorists: it is no enmity of yesterday; the imprecations that follow presuppose an inflexible obduracy on the side of the enemies.
entries.61e29de01eebbdb95db507969a2af7bd742d9f42: <reference osisRef="Ps.109.6-Ps.109.10">Psa 109:6-10</reference> <div eID="gen10053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10054" type="x-p"/> The writer now turns to one among the many, and in the angry zealous fervour of despised love calls down God’s judgment upon him. To call down a higher power, more particularly for punishment, upon any one is expressed by על (הפקיד) פּקד, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.3">Jer 15:3</reference>; Lev 26:16. The tormentor of innocence shall find a superior executor who will bring him before the tribunal (which is expressed in Latin by <hi type="italic">legis actio per manus injectionem</hi>). The judgment scene in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.109.6">Psa 109:6</reference></hi>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.109.7">Psa 109:7</reference></hi> shows that this is what is intended in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.109.6">Psa 109:6</reference></hi>: At the right hand is the place of the accuser, who in this instance will not rest before the <hi type="italic">damnatus</hi> <hi type="italic">es</hi> has been pronounced. He is called שׂטן, which is not to be understood here after <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.4">1Sa 29:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.22">2Sa 19:22</reference>, but after Zec 3:1; <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.1">1Ch 21:1</reference>, if not directly of Satan, still of a superhuman (cf. Num 22:22) being which opposes him, by appearing before God as his κατήγωρ; for according to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.109.7">Psa 109:7</reference></hi> the שׂטן is to be thought of as accuser, and according to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.109.7">Psa 109:7</reference></hi> God as Judge. רשׁע has the sense of <hi type="italic">reus</hi>, and יצא refers to the publication of the sentence. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.109.7">Psa 109:7</reference></hi> wishes that his prayer, viz., that by which he would wish to avert the divine sentence of condemnation, may become לחטאה, not: a missing of the mark, i.e., ineffectual (Thenius), but, according to the usual signification of the word: a sin, viz., because it proceeds from despair, not from true penitence. In <reference osisRef="Ps.109.8">Psa 109:8</reference> the incorrigible one is wished an untimely death (מעטּים as in one other instance, only, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.1">Ecc 5:1</reference>) and the loss of his office. The lxx renders: τὴν ἐπισκοπὴν αὐτοῦ λάβοι ἕτερος. פּקדּה really signifies the office of overseer, oversight, office, and the one individual must have held a prominent position among the enemies of the psalmist. Having died off from this position before his time, he shall leave behind him a family deeply reduced in circumstances, whose former dwelling - place-he was therefore wealthy - becomes “ruins.” His children wander up and down far from these ruins (מן as e.g., in Jdg 5:11; <reference osisRef="Job.28.4">Job 28:4</reference>) and beg (דּרשׁ, like προσαιτεῖν ἐπαιτεῖν, Sir. 40:28 = לחם בּקּשׁ, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.25">Psa 37:25</reference>). Instead of ודרשׁוּ the reading ודרשׁוּ is also found. A <hi type="italic">Poel</hi> is now and then formed from the strong verbs also,<note placement="foot">In connection with the strong verb it frequently represents the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> which does not occur, as with דּרשׁ, לשׁן, שׁפט, or even represents the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> which, as in the case of שׁרשׁ, is already made use of in another signification (<hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, to root out; <hi type="italic">Poel</hi>, to take root).</note> in the inflexion of which the <hi type="italic">Cholem</hi> is sometimes shortened to <hi type="italic">Kametz chatuph</hi>; vid., the forms of לשׁן, to slander, in <reference osisRef="Ps.101.5">Psa 101:5</reference>, תּאר, to sketch, mark out in outline, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.13">Isa 44:13</reference>, cf. also <reference osisRef="Job.20.26">Job 20:26</reference> (תּאכלהוּ) and <reference osisRef="Isa.62.9">Isa 62:9</reference> (according to the reading מאספיו). To read the <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi> in these instances as <hi type="italic">ā</hi>, and to regard these forms as resolved <hi type="italic">Piels</hi>, is, in connection with the absence of the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>, contrary to the meaning of the pointing; on purpose to guard against this way of reading it, correct codices have ודרשׁוּ (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.69.19">Psa 69:19</reference>), which Baer has adopted.
entries.7bdc4778a68796f4cfeb36721b4bc95f51ef95fc: <reference osisRef="Ps.109.11-Ps.109.15">Psa 109:11-15</reference> <div eID="gen10054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10055" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> נקּשׁ properly signifies to catch in snares; here, like the Arabic Arab. <hi type="italic">nqš</hi>, II, IV, corresponding to the Latin <hi type="italic">obligare</hi> (as referring to the creditor’s right of claim); nosheh is the name of the creditor as he who gives time for payment, gives credit (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.24.2">Isa 24:2</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Ps.109.12">Psa 109:12</reference> משׁך חסד, to draw out mercy, is equivalent to causing it to continue and last, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.11">Psa 36:11</reference>, cf. Jer 31:3. אחריתו, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.109.13">Psa 109:13</reference></hi>, does not signify his future, but as <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.109.13">Psa 109:13</reference></hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.37.38">Psa 37:38</reference>) shows: his posterity. יהי להכרית is not merely <hi type="italic">exscindatur</hi>, but <hi type="italic">exscindenda sit</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.16">Eze 30:16</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.2.6">Jos 2:6</reference>), just as in other instances חיה ל corresponds to the active <hi type="italic">fut. periphrasticum</hi>, e.g., <reference osisRef="Gen.15.12">Gen 15:12</reference>; Isa 37:26. With reference to ימּח instead of ימּח (contracted from ימּחה), vid., Ges. §75, rem. 8. A Jewish acrostic interpretation of the name ישׁוּ runs: ימּח שׁמו וזכרו. This curse shall overtake the family of the υἱὸς τῆς ἀπωλείας. All the sins of his parents and ancestors shall remain indelible above before God the Judge, and here below the race, equally guilty, shall be rooted out even to its memory, i.e., to the last trace of it.
entries.5840c0374e328e0293ecafd76608d2e2eabf2dbb: <reference osisRef="Ps.109.16-Ps.109.20">Psa 109:16-20</reference> <div eID="gen10055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10056" type="x-p"/> He whom he persecuted with a thirst for blood, was, apart from this, a great sufferer, bowed down and poor and נכאה לבב, of terrified, confounded heart. lxx κατανενυγμένον (Jerome, <hi type="italic">compunctum</hi>); but the stem-word is not נכא (נכה), root נך, but כּאה, Syriac <hi type="italic">bā'ā'</hi>, cogn. כּהה, to cause to come near, to meet. The verb, and more especially in <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>., is proved to be Hebrew by Dan 11:30. Such an one who without anything else is of a terrified heart, inasmuch as he has been made to feel the wrath of God most keenly, this man has persecuted with a deadly hatred. He had experienced kindness (חסד) in a high degree, but he blotted out of his memory that which he had experienced, not for an instant imagining that he too on his part had to exercise חסד. The <hi type="italic">Poel</hi> מותת instead of המית points to the agonizing death (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Isa 53:9</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.10">Eze 28:10</reference> מותי) to which he exposes God’s anointed. The fate of the shedder of blood is not expressed after the manner of a wish in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.16-Ps.109.18">Psa 109:16-18</reference>, but in the historical form, as being the result that followed of inward necessity from the matter of fact of the course which he had himself determined upon. The verb בּוא <hi type="italic">seq. acc</hi>. signifies to surprise, suddenly attack any one, as in Isa 41:25. The three figures in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.18">Psa 109:18</reference> are climactic: he has clothed himself in cursing, he has drunk it in like water (<reference osisRef="Job.15.16">Job 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.7">Job 34:7</reference>), it has penetrated even to the marrow of his bones, like the oily preparations which are rubbed in and penetrate to the bones.n In <reference osisRef="Ps.109.19">Psa 109:19</reference> the emphasis rests upon יעטּה and upon תּמיד. The summarizing <reference osisRef="Ps.109.20">Psa 109:20</reference> is the close of a strophe. פּעלּה, an earned reward, here punishment incurred, is especially frequent in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference>, e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.49.4">Psa 49:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.10">Psa 40:10</reference>; it also occurs once even in the Tôra, Lev 19:13. Those who answer the loving acts of the righteous with such malevolence in word and in deed commit a satanic sin for which there is no forgiveness. The curse is the fruit of their own choice and deed. Arnobius: <hi type="italic">Nota ex arbitrio evenisse ut nollet, propter haeresim, quae dicit Deum alios praedestinasse ad benedictionem, alios ad maledictionem.</hi>
entries.cd45f2ce9fc905994b1172bb8ff062119c3a66a4: <reference osisRef="Ps.109.21-Ps.109.25">Psa 109:21-25</reference> <div eID="gen10056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10057" type="x-p"/> The thunder and lightning are now as it were followed by a shower of tears of deep sorrowful complaint. Ps 109 here just as strikingly accords with Ps 69, as Ps 69 does with Ps 22 in the last strophe but one. The twofold name <hi type="italic">Jahve Adonaj</hi> (vid., <hi type="italic">Symbolae</hi>, p. 16) corresponds to the deep-breathed complaint. עשׂה אתּי, deal with me, i.e., succouring me, does not greatly differ from לי in 1Sa 14:6. The confirmation, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.109.21">Psa 109:21</reference></hi>, runs like <reference osisRef="Ps.69.17">Psa 69:17</reference> : Thy loving-kindness is טּוב, absolutely good, the ground of everything that is good and the end of all evil. Hitzig conjectures, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.17">Psa 69:17</reference>, חסדך כּטוב, “according to the goodness of Thy loving-kindness;” but this formula is without example: “for Thy loving-kindness is good” is a statement of the motive placed first and corresponding to the “for thy Name’s sake.” In <reference osisRef="Ps.109.22">Psa 109:22</reference> (a variation of <reference osisRef="Ps.55.5">Psa 55:5</reference>) חלל, not חלל, is traditional; this חלל, as being <hi type="italic">verb. denom.</hi> from חלל, signifies to be pierced, and is therefore equivalent to חולל (cf. <reference osisRef="Luke.2.35">Luk 2:35</reference>). The metaphor of the shadow in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.23">Psa 109:23</reference> is as in Psa 102:12. When the day declines, the shadow lengthens, it becomes longer and longer (Virgil, <hi type="italic">majoresque cadunt altis de montibus umbrae</hi>), till it vanishes in the universal darkness. Thus does the life of the sufferer pass away. The poet intentionally uses the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נהלכתּי (another reading is נהלכתּי); it is a power rushing upon him from without that drives him away thus after the manner of a shadow into the night. The locust or grasshopper (apart from the plague of the locusts) is proverbial as being a defenceless, inoffensive little creature that is soon driven away, Job 39:20. ננער, to be shaken out or off (cf. Arabic <hi type="italic">na‛ûra</hi>, a water-wheel that fills its clay-vessels in the river and empties them out above, and הנּער, Zec 11:16, where Hitzig wishes to read הנּער, <hi type="italic">dispulsio</hi> = <hi type="italic">dispulsi</hi>). The fasting in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.24">Psa 109:24</reference> is the result of the loathing of all food which sets in with deep grief. כּחשׁ משּׁמן signifies to waste away so that there is no more fat left.<note placement="foot">The verbal group כחשׁ, כחד, Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥajda , kaḥuṭa</hi>, etc. has the primary signification of withdrawal and taking away or decrease; to deny is the same as to withdraw from agreement, and he becomes thin from whom the fat withdraws, goes away. Saadia compares on this passage (פרה) בהמה כחושׁה, a lean cow, <hi type="italic">Berachoth</hi> 32 <hi type="italic">a</hi>. In like manner Targum II renders <reference osisRef="Gen.41.27">Gen 41:27</reference> תּורתא כהישׁתא, the lean kine.</note> <div eID="gen10057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10058" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.109.25">Psa 109:25</reference> אני is designedly rendered prominent: in this the form of his affliction he is the butt of their reproaching, and they shake their heads doubtfully, looking upon him as one who is punished of God beyond all hope, and giving him up for lost. It is to be interpreted thus after Psa 69:11.
entries.69bf6b7d58937501a10677142a42b925d99e5a03: <reference osisRef="Ps.109.26-Ps.109.31">Psa 109:26-31</reference> <div eID="gen10058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10059" type="x-p"/> The cry for help is renewed in the closing strophe, and the Psalm draws to a close very similarly to Ps 69 and Ps 22, with a joyful prospect of the end of the affliction. In <reference osisRef="Ps.109.27">Psa 109:27</reference> the hand of God stands in contrast to accident, the work of men, and his own efforts. All and each one will undeniably perceive, when God at length interposes, that it is His hand which here does that which was impossible in the eyes of men, and that it is His work which has been accomplished in this affliction and in the issue of it. He blesses him whom men curse: they arise without attaining their object, whereas His servant can rejoice in the end of his affliction. The futures in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.29">Psa 109:29</reference> are not now again imprecations, but an expression of believingly confident hope. In correct texts כּמעיל has <hi type="italic">Mem raphatum</hi>. The “many” are the “congregation” (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.22.23">Psa 22:23</reference>). In the case of the marvellous deliverance of this sufferer the congregation or church has the pledge of its own deliverance, and a bright mirror of the loving-kindness of its God. The sum of the praise and thanksgiving follows in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.31">Psa 109:31</reference>, where כּי signifies <hi type="italic">quod</hi>, and is therefore allied to the ὅτι <hi type="italic">recitativum</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.22.25">Psa 22:25</reference>). The three Good Friday Psalms all sum up the comfort that springs from David’s affliction for all suffering ones in just such a pithy sentence (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.25">Psa 22:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.34">Psa 69:34</reference>). Jahve comes forward at the right hand of the poor, contending for him (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.110.5">Psa 110:5</reference>), to save (him) from those who judge (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.33">Psa 37:33</reference>), i.e., condemn, his soul. The contrast between this closing thought and Psa 109:6. is unmistakeable. At the right hand of the tormentor stands Satan as an accuser, at the right hand of the tormented one stands God as his vindicator; he who delivered him over to human judges is condemned, and he who was delivered up is “taken away out of distress and from judgment” (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.8">Isa 53:8</reference>) by the Judge of the judges, in order that, as we now hear in the following Psalm, he may sit at the right hand of the heavenly King. Ἐδικαιώθη ἐν πνεύματι...ἀνελήμφθη ἐν δόξῃ! (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>).  <chapter eID="Ps.109"/> <div eID="gen10059" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 109
This psalm consists of three parts. It begins with a complaint; next follows an enumeration of various imprecations; and then comes a prayer with an expression of true gratitude. And although David here complains of the injuries which he sustained, yet, as he was a typical character, everything that is expressed in the psalm must properly be applied to Christ, the Head of the Church, and to all the faithful, inasmuch as they are his members; so that when unjustly treated and tormented by their enemies, they may apply to God for help, to whom vengeance belongs.
From the express application of a part of this awfully prophetic poem to Judas by the Apostle Peter, (Acts 1:20) we learn that the punishment and sufferings of that unhappy man form its subject. It has also been justly viewed as shadowing forth, not merely the fate of the wretched Iscariot, and his immediate associates, but the dreadful and justly-merited destiny of the Jewish polity and nation. “The first five verses of this psalm,” says Horsley, “clearly describe the treatment which our Lord met with from the Jews. The curses that follow as clearly describe the judgments which have fallen upon that miserable people. So that the whole is a prediction of his sufferings, and of their punishment, delivered in the form of complaint and imprecation.” Whatever, therefore, may be said as to the primary reference of the psalm to the lamentations and denunciations poured forth by David, in consequence of the perfidy and cruelty of some inveterate foe, Christ must be principally understood as the person who gives utterance to these lamentations and denunciations, occasioned by the injurious treatment he received from his betrayer and murderers. — See Appendix.
Psalm 109:1-5
To the Chief Musician, a Psalm of David.
1. O God of my praise! be not silent; 2. Because the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of deceit are opened upon me: they have spoken against me with the tongue of guile. 3. And they have encompassed me with the words of hatred, and have contended with me without cause. 4. On account of my love they have been opposed to me; but I gave myself to prayer. 5. They rendered to me evil for good, and hatred for love.
 
1 O God of my praise! be not silent In these words, which may be considered as an introduction to the psalm, David declares that he neither could find nor would desire any other than God to stand forward in vindication of the integrity of his heart. For in denominating him the God of his praise, he intrusts to him the vindication of his innocence, in the face of the calumnies by which he was all but universally assailed. Some are of opinion that this clause is to be understood as referring to David’s having actually declared that he himself was the publisher of God’s praises; but the scope of the passage is opposed to such an interpretation; for we find David appealing to the judgment of God against the unjust and cruel hatred to which he was subjected in the world. There is in the words an implied contrast, because, when calumny is rampant, innocence is duly and properly estimated by none but God only. The meaning of the passage is this: Lord, although I may be regarded as the vilest of the vile, and exposed to the reproach of the world, yet thou wilt maintain the uprightness of my character, and on this account thou wilt also set forth my praise.
The Septuagint and Vulgate attach the same meaning to the Psalmist’s prayer. The reading of the former being, Ω Θεὸς τὴν αἴνεσίν μου μὴ παρασιωπήσης, and that of the latter, “Deus, laudem meam ne tacueris,” O God! be not silent of my praise. The phrase, as it stands in the Hebrew text, is, however, capable of a double signification; for it may refer either to God’s praising David, or to David’s praising God. In the one case, it will intimate that God was the object of his praise; in which sense it is said, Deuteronomy 10:21, “He is thy praise, and He is thy God,” and will mean, Be not silent to refuse, neglect not my praising of thee. In the other sense the prayer is, as our author states, Whilst others reproach me, be not silent of my praise, be thou my advocate, plead my causes, proclaim and justify my innocence.
This interpretation corresponds well with that which is immediately subjoined, be not silent For when we are overwhelmed by the aspersions of the wicked, it would surely be improper on the part of God, who is the witness of our innocence, to remain silent. At the same time, what I formerly stated must not be forgotten, that while David mourns over the injuries which he in particular was suffering, yet, in his own person, he represented Christ, and the whole body of his Church. From this we are taught, when we are subjected to every species of indignity by men, to repose with perfect confidence under the protection of God alone. No man, however, can, with sincerity of heart, surrender himself entirely into the hand of God, except he has first formed the resolution of treating with contempt the reproaches of the world, and is also fully persuaded that he has God as the defender of his cause.

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Be turned into sin, or be imputed to him as his sin, or be as unavailable with God for his relief as his sins. When he makes supplication to his Judge, as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> speaks <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 9. 15. for pity and pardon, let him be the more provoked and enraged by it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. Let his days <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The days of his life. Let him die an untimely death.</ns0:note> be few, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Act. 1. 20.</ns0:note> let another take his <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> charge.</ns0:note> office <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Made void by his death. He also implies that his enemy was a man of power and reputation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. Let his children be fatherless <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Whilst they are but children, and so unable to provide for themselves.</ns0:note>, and his wife a widow <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either made a widow by his death: or constantly a widow; all persons abhorring her who was re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lated to so vile a miscreant.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. Let his children be continually vaga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bonds <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Having no certain place of abode. Which is a grievous curse in it self, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 4. 12, 14. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 16. 2.</ns0:note>, and beg <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">This increa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />seth their misery.</ns0:note>: let them seek <ns0:hi>their bread</ns0:hi> also out of their desolate places <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Into which they are fled for fear and shame, as not daring to shew their faces amongst men.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11. Let the extortioner <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>usurer,</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>creditor.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> catch <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>Ensnare,</ns0:hi> which is an Emphatical expression, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> take away not only by oppressi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on and violence, but also by cheats and cunning artifices, where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by such persons entangle, and so ruine their debtors.</ns0:note> all that he hath: and let the stranger <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Who hath no right to his goods, and will use no pity nor measure in spoiling him.</ns0:note> spoil his labour <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">All the fruits of his labours.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. Let there be none to <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 34. 10.</ns0:note> extend mercy unto him: neither let there be any to favour his fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />therless children <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Let him and his be unpitied and hated as the publick enemies of mankind.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 18. 19.</ns0:note> Let his posterity be cut off, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> in the generation following <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>in another generation,</ns0:hi> either in the third genera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion: or in the second, or that which next followed the ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neration of his fathers. So in this clause he limits the time of that destruction which he imprecates or foretells in the former.</ns0:note> let their name be blotted out.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14. Let the iniquity of his fathers be remem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bred <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Against him, or punished in him, as God hath threat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned to deal with great delinquents, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20. 5.</ns0:note> with the LORD, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15. Let them <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The sins of his parents last mentioned.</ns0:note> be before the LORD <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">In Gods sight and memory to provoke God to punish him: let them not be covered or pardoned.</ns0:note> con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinually, that he may <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 18. 17. Psal. 34. 16.</ns0:note> cut off the memory of them from the earth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16. Because that he remembred not <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">His duty to God, and his obligation to me for my for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer kindness expressed <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4, 5.</ns0:note> to shew mercy, but persecuted the poor and needy man <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">My self, who was deso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />late and miserable, whose condition required pity and not additions of cruelty.</ns0:note>, that he might even s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ay the broken in heart <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Whose spirit was grieved and even broken with the burden of his calamities.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:499" />17. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezek. 35. 6.</ns0:note> As he loved cursing <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either, 1. cursed or sinful courses. Or rather, 2. to curse others, as appears from the blessing here opposed to it, and from the next verse; to wish and to procure mischief to others, and especially to me.</ns0:note>, so let it come unto him: as he delighted not in blessing <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">In desiring and promoting the welfare of others, which indeed was an eye-sore and tor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment to him.</ns0:note>, so let it be far from him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. As he clothed himself with cursing like as with a garment <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Which a man wears constantly, and that as an orna<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment.</ns0:note>: so let it come <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> within him.</ns0:note> into his bowels like water <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Which when a man drinks, goes into his bowels, and searcheth all the inwards of his belly.</ns0:note>, and like oyl <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Which is more piercing than water, and being applied to outward parts, reacheth even to the bones and marrow.</ns0:note> into his bones.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19. Let it be unto him as the garment <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> covereth him, and for a girdle <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Which cleaves closer and faster to a man than a garment, especially than the Eastern garments did, which were large and loose.</ns0:note> wherewith he is girded continually.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20. <ns0:hi>Let</ns0:hi> this <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>work.</ns0:hi> Isai. 40. 10.</ns0:note> reward of mine adversa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ries <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Of those who were confederate with that arch-enemy in his wicked enterprise.</ns0:note> from the LORD, and of them that speak evil against my soul <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">With design to take away my life.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21. But do thou for me <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">To wit, what I desire, which he expresseth in the next clause. Or, <ns0:hi>do thou act for me:</ns0:hi> be not silent or still, but stir up thy self to work on my behalf.</ns0:note>, O GOD the LORD, for thy names sake <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">For the glory of thy faithfulness, which is highly concerned in giving me the de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liverance which thou hast promised to me.</ns0:note>: because thy mercy is good <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Graci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous, and ready to do good to all, but especially to those that love and fear thee. As <ns0:hi>sin</ns0:hi> is said to be <ns0:hi>sinful, Rom.</ns0:hi> 7. 13. so Gods mercy may be said to be merciful, to wit, in an eminent degree, and above the mercy of all the creatures.</ns0:note>, deliver thou me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22. For I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> poor and needy <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">And therefore a very proper object for thy pity and help.</ns0:note>, and my heart is wounded within me <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">I am wounded not slightly, but even to the very heart with soul-piercing sorrows.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23. I am gone <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>I am made to go,</ns0:hi> either, 1. from place to place; which was <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> case when he was persecuted by <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> and by <ns0:hi>Absalom;</ns0:hi> and Christs case upon earth, where he had no certain place <ns0:hi>where to lay his head, Mat.</ns0:hi> 8. 20. Or, 2. into the grave, as this phrase is used 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 17. 11. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 58. 9. and oft elsewhere.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 102. 11.</ns0:note> like the shadow, when it declineth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Towards the evening, when, the Sun setting, it vanisheth instantly, and irrecoverably until the Sun rise again, which it never will do to me in this world, when once I am gone out of it.</ns0:note>: I am tossed up and down as the lo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cust <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Which of it self is unstable, con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinually skipping from place to place, and is easily driven away with every wind. So am I exposed to perpetual and successive changes within my self, and to a thousand violen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces and mischiefs from other persons and things.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24. My knees are weak through <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>asting <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either with voluntary fasts, to which the frequency and long continuance of my calamities obliged me: or with for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ced fasts sometimes through want of necessary provisions, but most commonly from that loathing of meat, which was occa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sioned by his excessive sorrows and terrors. See on <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 107. 18.</ns0:note>: and my flesh faileth of fatness <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>for want of fatness.</ns0:hi> See the like Hebrew phrases <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 18. 26. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 48. 45. <ns0:hi>Lam.</ns0:hi> 4. 9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25. I became also a reproach unto them <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Instead of that pity, which either Religion or Humanity should have taught them to a man in extreme misery, they loaded me with reproaches and scorns.</ns0:note>: when they looked upon me, they shaked their heads <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">A gesture of con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tempt and derision: of which see <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 16. 4. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 22 8.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26. Help me, O LORD my God: O save me according to thy mercy:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27. That they may know <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Being convinced of the eminency and singularity and strangeness of the work.</ns0:note> that this <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy hand: <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> thou, LORD, hast done it.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28. Let them curse <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">I can patiently bear their curses, as being causless and fully compensated by thy blessing. Or, <ns0:hi>they do and will curse,</ns0:hi> I expect nothing else from them.</ns0:note>, but bless thou: when they arise <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Bestir themselves against me. Both God and men are oft said to <ns0:hi>arise</ns0:hi> when they enter upon any undertaking, as <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 24. 9. <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 8. 21. 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 13. 6. & 21. 4, &c.</ns0:note> let them be ashamed, but let thy servant rejoyce.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29. Let mine adversaries be clothed with shame <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">For the disappointment of their wicked hopes and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />signs, and for that unexpected destruction which they have brought upon themselves.</ns0:note>: and let them cover themselves with their own confusion, as with a mantle.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30. I will greatly praise the LORD <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">For that deliverance which I confidently expect.</ns0:note> with my mouth: yea, I will praise him among the multitude <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>among the mighty</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>great men,</ns0:hi> as this word sometimes signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fies. Comp. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 119. 46.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31. For he shall stand at the right hand of the poor <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">To defend him from his adversary, who stood in that place to accuse him, and to procure his condemnation and destruction. See above on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6.</ns0:note>, to save <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> from the judges of his soul.</ns0:note> from those that condemn his soul <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That pass a sentence of death upon him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
